title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 1: A Renaissance in the Judiciary
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- the Closing Statement CJP delivered June 11, 2001 (the SC's exact 100th birthday) at the final lecture of Phase I of the Centenary Lecture Series, which he hailed as 'the fulcrum of the celebrations'

A survey of the Centenary Lecture Series (begun July 11, 2000): past (Narvasa on 'The Chief Justices in Philippine History'; Fernando on a century of constitutionalism), the women of the bench (Melencio Herrera), inclusion (Mastura on Shari'ah law), foreign luminaries (Israel's Beinisch, Hungary's Solt), and current jurisprudential trends

The 'Davide Watch' and the Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR): CJ Davide's reform vision announced Nov 30, 1998 -- a judiciary that is independent, effective, efficient and worthy of public trust, and a legal profession that is ethical, accessible and cost-effective; backed by a concrete day-by-day development plan and international donors

The framing thesis: a centenary cannot be justified by rehashing past successes or gloating over the present; it must set forth collective dreams of the future -- a 'renaissance in the judiciary' driven by reform
sub_topics: The Centenary Lecture Series as 'the fulcrum of the celebrations,' one of more than 50 centenary activities; CJP's Closing Statement reproduced as Chapter 1

The opening lecture: former CJ Andres R. Narvasa, 'The Chief Justices in Philippine History' (July 11, 2000); retired CJ Enrique M. Fernando, 'A Century of Constitutionalism: The Mission (per Malcolm, J.) and Its Fulfillment (per Laurel, J.)'

Women on the bench: Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera, 'Feminine Grace, the High Court and Jurisprudence' -- 'though outnumbered, the lady justices were never out-written, out-argued or out-achieved by the men'
Inclusion of the Muslim legal tradition: Prof. Michael O. Mastura, 'Shari'ah Law and the Philippine Legal System' (Sept 12, 2000)

Foreign legal luminaries on the universality of human-rights principles: Justice Dorit Beinisch (Israel), 'Protecting Civil Liberties in a State of Continuing Emergency'; Dr. Pal Solt (Hungary), 'Function of the Supreme Court of Justice in Hungary'

Four lectures on current jurisprudential trends: Cong. Leandro B. Verceles Jr. (E-Commerce contracts), Dr. Franklin M. Zweig (Life Technologies and the Rule of Law), 'an incumbent member of the Court whose name need not be mentioned' (Old Doctrines and New Paradigms -- CJP himself, i.e., Chapter 2), and a panel of Raul Pangalangan, Katrina Legarda and Randy David (Impact of People Power)

The 'Davide Watch': the judiciary-at-the-new-millennium reform program announced on CJ Davide's assumption Nov 30, 1998 -- 'inspired by Scripture, born of idealism, but grounded on the reality of the possible'; complemented by the Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR)

APJR's international and domestic support: the Philippine government and local donors plus the UN Development Fund, World Bank, Asia Foundation, UNICEF, ADB, and bilateral aid from Japan, Canada, Australia, the US and the Netherlands

Davide's reform vision quoted: 'a judiciary that is independent, effective and efficient, and worthy of public trust and confidence; and a legal profession that provides quality, ethical, accessible and cost-effective legal service'
The 'trouble with hello is goodbye' close: while the pre-centenary lecture series ends, its influence and memory will endure as a 'renaissance in the judiciary'
signature_phrases: though outnumbered, the lady justices were never out-written, out-argued or out-achieved by the men

stances.claim: A centenary 'cannot be justified by a mere rehash of past successes or by an overextended gloating over the present'; its true purpose is to 'set forth our collective dreams of the future.' The celebration is legitimate only insofar as it advances the ongoing reform of the judiciary, not as nostalgia.
stances.rhetorical_move: future-orientation-as-the-justification-of-commemoration: reframing a centennial from retrospective celebration into a launching point for reform
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing rationale for the entire centenary

stances.claim: The 'Davide Watch' reform program is not 'merely a broad statement of intent and principles' but is 'complemented by a definite development plan implemented day by day' through the APJR, with concrete domestic and international support -- distinguishing genuine institutional reform from aspirational rhetoric.
stances.rhetorical_move: plan-versus-rhetoric distinction: reform legitimated by an operational day-by-day program and funded backing rather than by stated principles alone
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's endorsement of the Davide reform program

notable_anecdotes: The series' symbolic arc: it was opened by the immediate past Chief Justice (Narvasa, on the past) and closed by the incumbent (Davide's vision, on the future), with the lectures in between extolling the present -- a deliberate past-present-future structure CJP highlights as significant.

The unnamed lecturer: Chapter 1 lists 'Old Doctrines and New Paradigms' as delivered by 'an incumbent member of the Court whose name need not be mentioned' -- a coy self-reference, since that lecturer was CJP himself and the lecture is Chapter 2 of the very same book.

The women of the bench: Melencio Herrera's lecture 'Feminine Grace, the High Court and Jurisprudence' is praised with the line that 'though outnumbered, the lady justices were never out-written, out-argued or out-achieved by the men.'

The closing song motif: CJP builds the peroration around the line 'the trouble with hello is goodbye,' arguing that while the lecture series must end, 'no curtain will be drawn' on the reform program it inaugurated.

Bench, bar, academe and reform partners following the APJR

decision_framework_signals: future-orientation-as-commemoration: a centenary justified by the reform it launches, not by nostalgia
plan-versus-rhetoric: reform credibility resting on a day-by-day operational program (APJR) with funded backing
universality-of-rights: foreign-luminary lectures invoked to show that human-rights principles transcend territorial law
one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the Closing Statement Justice Panganiban delivered on June 11, 2001 -- the Supreme Court's exact 100th birthday -- at the final lecture of Phase I of the Centenary Lecture Series, which he calls 'the fulcrum of the celebrations' among the Court's 50-plus centenary activities. He surveys the series begun July 11, 2000: former CJ Andres R. Narvasa opened it with 'The Chief Justices in Philippine History'; retired CJ Enrique M. Fernando spoke on a century of constitutionalism; Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera honored the women of the bench in 'Feminine Grace, the High Court and Jurisprudence' ('though outnumbered, the lady justices were never out-written, out-argued or out-achieved by the men'); Prof. Michael O. Mastura addressed 'Shari'ah Law and the Philippine Legal System'; and foreign luminaries Justice Dorit Beinisch of Israel and Dr. Pal Solt of Hungary spoke on civil liberties and the role of supreme courts, illustrating the universality of human-rights principles. Four lectures treated current jurisprudential trends -- including 'Old Doctrines and New Paradigms' by 'an incumbent member of the Court whose name need not be mentioned' (CJP himself, the book's Chapter 2). CJP frames the series as a deliberate past-present-future arc, closed by the incumbent Chief Justice's reform vision. He extols the 'Davide Watch' -- the judiciary-at-the-new-millennium program announced on CJ Davide's assumption on November 30, 1998, 'inspired by Scripture, born of idealism, but grounded on the reality of the possible' -- stressing that it is not 'merely a broad statement of intent' but is 'complemented by a definite development plan implemented day by day' through the Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR), backed by the UN Development Fund, World Bank, Asia Foundation, UNICEF, ADB, and bilateral aid from Japan, Canada, Australia, the US and the Netherlands. His governing thesis: a centenary 'cannot be justified by a mere rehash of past successes or by an overextended gloating over the present' but must 'set forth our collective dreams of the future.' He closes on the song line 'the trouble with hello is goodbye,' insisting that while the lecture series must end, its influence will endure as 'a well-remembered renaissance in the judiciary.'
